client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Last time we talked, you'd set a goal around cutting back on weeknights. How have things been going since then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Better than I expected, I think. Like, Monday through Wednesday I actually... I didn't drink at all. Which, you know, that's kind of a big deal for me. I wasn't white-knuckling it or anything. It just felt... manageable, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three nights in a row — that's real follow-through. You set a goal and you actually did it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah but... I mean, then Thursday happened. And it kind of... I don't know if 'unraveled' is the right word but. It wasn't great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about Thursday.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was this parent complaint. Kid's mom called the principal, said I'd embarrassed her son in front of the class. Which I — okay, maybe I was short with him, but I had a splitting headache and he would not stop talking during a test. And then the principal pulls me in and I just... I felt like everyone was watching me, you know? And when I got home I poured a drink. Then another one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the pressure kept stacking up — feeling scrutinized, maybe embarrassed — and when you got home, the drink felt like the one thing that was going to take the edge off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not like I blacked out or anything. I had three drinks, maybe four. Went to bed at a normal time. Showed up the next day. I just — I don't understand why every slip is treated like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's like nothing I do is ever enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it feel like when you hear it described as a slip?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like someone's keeping score. Like I did five good days and one bad one and the bad one is all that counts. That's — I'm sorry, that's just frustrating. I'm not trying to be difficult here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want the hard work to get erased by one rough night. That feels deeply unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I just — I thought I was doing better. And then it happened and I'm back to feeling like... I keep thinking about what my colleague said when she pulled me aside. The way she looked at me. Like she felt sorry for me. That's not — that's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The person you want to be still matters to you. That's actually one of the things that's kept you coming back here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My students are twelve, thirteen years old. And I'm standing up there talking about making good choices, being responsible... and meanwhile I'm nursing a headache before first period because I had too much the night before. I mean... what am I doing. What am I actually doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you want for yourself in that classroom?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to actually be present. Not just... showing up and going through the motions. I used to really enjoy teaching. There were days I'd leave school feeling good — like I actually connected with a kid, made something click for them. I haven't felt that in a while. And I think I know why.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see a version of yourself that's more present — and you can also see what's been getting in the way of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't want to throw away the whole week because of Thursday, you know? Like, three good days, two okay, one bad — that's still better than where I was two months ago. Right? I think that's right. I need that to still count for something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in today with something real — three nights without drinking, which hasn't happened in a long time. Thursday was hard. Work piled up, you felt cornered, and the drinking felt like the fastest way out. That left you feeling like you'd failed, and when you thought about your students it stung. But underneath all of that, there's still someone who knows exactly what he wants — to show up, to connect, to feel good leaving work. And that person isn't ready to quit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not. I mean — some days it feels impossible, I'm not gonna pretend otherwise. But... no. I'm not ready to give up on this.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in today. I know this probably wasn't how you planned to spend your Thursday. Your wife mentioned she was worried about you — I'd like to hear your side of things. What brings you here from where you're sitting?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? She overreacted. I mean, I appreciate that she cares, I do, but... I'm a teacher. I've been doing this for eleven years. I manage thirty kids at a time, I grade papers at ten o'clock at night, I — look, I have a drink in the evening to decompress. That's not a crisis. That's just... adulting, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eleven years in the classroom — that's not nothing. You're clearly someone who takes his work seriously, and that kind of pressure is real. What I'm curious about is what the evenings actually look like for you. Not judging, just want to understand.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home around four-thirty, sometimes five if there's a meeting. I'll... pour a glass of wine, or sometimes a couple of beers, while I'm making dinner. And then maybe another one after. It's — I don't know, it's the only part of the day where nobody needs anything from me. My wife's got the kids, the house quiets down a little, and I just... exhale. Is that so bad?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment of exhale — sounds like it's become pretty essential to getting through the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. And I know how that sounds. I'm not stupid — I teach health class, I know the talking points. But knowing something and, uh, and feeling something are different things. Some mornings I wake up and I'm not — I'm not great. And I tell myself I'll cut back, and then by four o'clock I'm counting down the minutes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something important — that some mornings you're not great, and that you've already been trying to cut back on your own. That takes some honesty to admit. I want to ask you directly: how often are those rough mornings happening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. More than I'd like. A few times a week, maybe. I had — okay, there was one day last month where I probably shouldn't have driven. I knew it but I did it anyway and nothing happened, but... I think about that. I do think about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet you got in the car.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Don't — look, I know. You don't have to say it like that. I know what I did. I'm not proud of it. But I also didn't wrap my car around a tree and I got to school and I taught my classes and nobody got hurt. So can we just — can we not make that the whole conversation?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. I hear you — you don't want to be defined by one bad decision. What I'm noticing though is that you brought it up yourself, unprompted. Part of you put that on the table for a reason.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I don't know why I said that. Maybe I just — maybe I'm tired of carrying it around. My colleague pulled me aside two weeks ago. She didn't say anything mean, she was actually really kind about it, but... I could see it in her face. She could smell it on me. At seven-thirty in the morning. And I stood there and I smiled and I said I'd had a bad night's sleep. And she nodded like she believed me. She didn't believe me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lonely place to be — keeping up appearances in front of the people you work with every day. What does it cost you to keep doing that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. I mean... not everything, I still have my job, my family. But it's like — I used to really love teaching. Like, genuinely. I'd stay late, I'd come up with these projects, the kids were... I was good at it. And now I'm just getting through. I'm just surviving until the end of the day so I can go home and pour a drink and feel like myself again for two hours. And even that's not really working anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The thing you built your identity around — being a good teacher — you can feel it slipping. And the drinking that started as a way to cope is now part of what's pulling it away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it out loud it sounds so obvious. Like, why didn't I just — why did it take this long? My wife has been patient. More than I deserve, honestly. My kids are seven and nine. They notice things. My son asked me last week why my breath smells funny at bedtime. I told him it was mouthwash.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard today, because I think it matters. You came in ready to defend yourself — and I get it, nobody wants to be here. But in the last forty minutes you've told me about a morning you drove impaired, a colleague who saw through you, evenings where the only way you feel like yourself is through alcohol, and a seven-year-old you lied to. That's not a man who doesn't care. That's a man who's been fighting this alone for a long time. What would it mean for you to not have to fight it alone anymore?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I think... I think it would feel like relief? I've been so focused on not being found out that I forgot there was a version of this where I actually get better. Is that — is that actually possible? At this point?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yes. Unambiguously yes. You're thirty-seven, you have insight, you have people in your corner, and you walked in here today. Those aren't small things. What I'd like to do is talk about what a next step might actually look like — something concrete, not overwhelming. What feels like the most manageable place to start?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Telling my wife the truth, I think. The whole truth. She knows something's wrong but she doesn't know how wrong. I've been protecting her from it, but... maybe I've just been protecting myself. Yeah. I think I start there.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I want you to know this is a pretty open space — no agenda, no pressure. I understand someone brought you here, and I'm just curious, what's your sense of... why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I didn't want to come. My sister called this place and basically — I don't know, she decided I have a problem. I don't think I have a problem. She's the one who has a problem. Always interfering from back home like she can see my whole life through a phone screen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this really wasn't your idea. I'm wondering — what would you want me to understand about your life that you don't think your sister gets?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She doesn't understand anything. She has her husband, her kids, her friends down the street — everything. She calls me once a week and suddenly she's an expert. I'm here alone. Like, completely alone. And I have a drink sometimes to unwind. So what? People drink.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She has a whole world around her, and from where you're standing, it doesn't feel like she really sees what your day-to-day life is actually like here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. She heard my voice one time and decided I needed to be fixed. I was just tired. I'm always tired. That doesn't mean I'm an alcoholic or whatever. I just — people cope. I'm coping.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you're always tired — what does a typical week actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I work. I come home. I, um... make food sometimes. Watch things on my phone. There's no one here. My English is okay but it's not the same, you know? At work everyone is nice but at five o'clock they go to their families and I go back to my apartment and it's just... very quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You built a whole life in a new country, by yourself, different language, different culture — that takes real courage. And what I'm hearing underneath all of this is that the quiet of that apartment has become... hard to be in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is hard. I didn't expect it to be this hard. I was so excited to come here, I thought I was ready. And now I just... I feel like I disappeared. Like no one knows I exist.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Feeling like you disappeared — that's a really striking way to put it. What does the drinking do for that feeling, when it comes?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It quiets it. The loneliness, the noise in my head — it gets smaller. For a little while. And then in the morning it's bigger than before and I feel terrible but... at least for a few hours I'm not feeling it. Is that awful? It sounds awful when I say it like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found something that gives you a break from a pain that nobody around you seems to understand. And at the same time — you're hearing yourself say it out loud right now, and something about that feels different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I don't know. I've never really said it like that before. Back home you don't — you don't talk about feelings, you just keep going. But I've been keeping going for two years and I'm so tired of it. Of pretending I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to bring together what you've shared. You came here feeling like it was unfair — because your sister isn't living what you're living. But underneath that frustration, there's something real: two years of building a life completely alone, no one who really knows you, and drinking has been the one thing that gives you some relief. And right now, something in you is questioning whether that relief is... enough.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. It's not enough. I think I knew that already. I think it was just easier to be angry at my sister than to actually — sit with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you if you didn't feel so invisible here? Like if that were actually possible — what might that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible. But there's a community center near my apartment, they have these cultural evenings, I've walked past it maybe ten times and never gone in. I keep thinking, what's the point, what if no one talks to me. But I keep walking past it, so... I don't know why I keep doing that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You keep walking past it. That's not nothing. That's a part of you that hasn't stopped looking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Maybe. I think I'm more scared of hoping than I am of just being alone. Does that make sense? Like if I try and it doesn't work then it's worse. But maybe... I don't know. Maybe I don't want the drinking to be the only thing that helps anymore.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this wasn't exactly your idea, so I want to be upfront — I'm not here to lecture you or tell you there's something wrong with you. My name's Dr. Reyes. Is it alright if we use first names?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure. Whatever. Mark's fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, Mark. Given that this was court-ordered — what's going through your head right now, sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? That it's a waste of time. I had one incident — one — and now I'm jumping through hoops like I'm some kind of... I'm not some alcoholic off the street. I'm a grown man who went through a rough couple of months and made a bad call. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting, this whole thing feels disproportionate. Like the system got involved in something that was... personal.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Four months ago my wife — ex-wife — decided she was done. Twenty-two years. Just... done. So I've been having a few drinks at night to take the edge off, and yeah, I made a mistake getting behind the wheel. I own that. But that doesn't make me an alcoholic, it makes me a guy who's been having the worst year of his life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. And then the divorce, and now this on top of it. That's a staggering amount of loss compressed into a very short time. I want you to know — I hear that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Nobody else does. Court doesn't. My ex sure as hell doesn't. Look, I'm handling it. The drinking — it's just... it's situational. It's not like I'm drinking at work or anything. I wait until I get home. I'm functional.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got real structure around it — waiting until you're home, keeping it out of work. Help me understand what a typical evening looks like for you these days.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home, pour a drink, watch TV. Maybe... more than one drink. And I used to call my kids every night but I — I've been calling less lately because I don't want them hearing me like that. But that's temporary, that's just until things settle down. I'm not — it's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand, the drinking gives you some relief at the end of hard days. And on the other — you just told me you're pulling back from your own kids because of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, yeah, when you put it like that it sounds bad. But I'm protecting them. I don't want them — my son Danny, he's thirteen, he doesn't need to hear his dad slurring on the phone. So I'm being responsible. That's... that IS responsible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're protecting him. What's it like for you, those nights when you don't call?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... it's fine. I mean... he used to call me, you know? He'd just call to tell me some stupid thing about school or whatever. Now it's me chasing him and he's always busy. I know he's a teenager. But I keep thinking — what does he think of me right now. With everything. The DUI. All of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're scared of losing him too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...My dad was a drunk. Like, a real one. And I swore I would never — I coached Danny's little league. Three years. I was there. I was always there. And now I'm sitting here and I... I don't know what he thinks when he looks at me anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mark, I want to reflect back what I'm hearing — because I think it matters. You walked in here angry, feeling like this was all unfair, like you were being treated as something you're not. And underneath that, there's a guy who is in real pain. Who lost his marriage, who's watching his relationship with his son change in ways he's frightened by, and who — somewhere — is aware that the drinking is connected to all of it. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that... I haven't really said any of that out loud before. To anyone. I've just been — I come home and I pour a drink and I don't have to think about it for a while. But it doesn't actually — it doesn't fix anything, does it. I wake up and it's all still there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It took real honesty to say that. What would it mean — for you, for Danny — if you started to actually look at this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want my son to be proud of me. That's... that's the thing. I don't want to be my dad. I don't know what any of this looks like yet, but — I think I need to figure it out. Before I lose him too.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to meet you. I'm glad you made it in today — I know coming in after detox is no small thing. Before we dive into anything heavy, how are you feeling right now, like physically, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... tired. Kind of shaky still. I don't know, I feel like I've been hit by a truck and then the truck backed up and hit me again. Which is basically what detox is, so. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The truck backed up — yeah, that's about right. And honestly, the fact that you're sitting here three days out of detox instead of... not sitting here, that actually tells me something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Don't go making me out to be some kind of hero. I'm here because my sister basically threatened to stop talking to me if I didn't go. So. I'm not sure I'd call it, like, strength or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. So she put pressure on you. And yet — you could've said no to her. People do. What made you actually follow through?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I just... something happened. Like, a few weeks ago I woke up on my bathroom floor and I had no idea what day it was. I thought it was Saturday, it was Tuesday. I'd missed two days of work. And I just sat there on the floor and I thought — this is... this is it. This is what it looks like now. And it scared me. I don't know. Maybe I don't wanna be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment on the bathroom floor — not knowing what day it was — something shifted. Like you saw yourself from the outside for a second and you didn't like what you saw.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And then I... I mean, I've done therapy before, it didn't help. So I'm not exactly — I'm sitting here but I'm not gonna pretend I think this is gonna fix anything. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: None taken, seriously. I'd rather you be honest with me than polite. What happened with therapy before — like what made it not work?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was just... the guy kept asking me about my childhood and my dad and whatever, and I'd leave feeling worse than when I came in. And I'm like, what's the point? I'm depressed, I drink too much, that's the problem — I don't need to excavate my entire childhood to figure out that life sucks sometimes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds exhausting — going in already feeling low, getting dug up even more, and then walking out carrying more weight than you brought. That's a legitimate reason to stop going. I want you to know that's not what this is going to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. So what is it then? Because I've heard that before too. 'This will be different.' And then it's the same worksheets and the same... 'how did that make you feel' stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Honestly? You get to decide what this is. I'm not here with an agenda for you. You mentioned the depression and the drinking — you see those as connected?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... obviously. Like when I feel like garbage, I drink. And then I feel like garbage again. And then I drink more. I'm not an idiot, I know how the cycle works. Knowing it doesn't really make it stop, though.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've mapped it out really clearly — the depression feeds the drinking, the drinking feeds the depression. And knowing the loop doesn't break the loop. That takes a lot of self-awareness to see that in yourself, especially right now when you're still physically recovering.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean... I've had a lot of time to think about it. Especially the last few weeks. I keep asking myself like, what am I actually doing this for. Not the drinking — like, what am I doing any of it for. My job, my apartment... I'm 39 and I feel like I'm just... going through motions. The alcohol was the only thing that made me feel like I wasn't just waiting to die. Which sounds really bad when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound bad. It sounds honest. And that — what you just said — that's actually really important. You weren't just drinking for drinking's sake. It was doing something for you. Taking the edge off... the emptiness, maybe?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. The emptiness. That's... yeah, that's a good word for it. And now I'm sitting here without it and the emptiness is just... it's very loud right now. I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I've heard today, because I think you've actually said a lot. You had a moment — the bathroom floor, Tuesday morning — that cracked something open. You're skeptical of this process and you have real reasons for that. You can see the cycle clearly. And underneath all of it, there's this emptiness that the alcohol was covering, and right now that's sitting there unprotected. That's a lot to carry into a first session. And you're still here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm still here. Yeah. I... don't know what that means yet. But. Yeah.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know sitting here might feel a little strange, especially after everything you've been through this past week. What brought you in — what's going on for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My coach, basically. [laughs bitterly] Like, I didn't just decide to show up here on my own. He gave me this whole speech about the team and whatever. I don't have a drinking problem. I'm twenty — this is what people do in college. Everyone drinks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So a big part of you is here because of your coach's ultimatum... not really because you chose this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And I just finished the detox thing — which was... whatever — and now I have to do therapy on top of it? I'm not some alcoholic. My dad's an alcoholic. I grew up watching that. I know what it looks like, and that is not me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've seen real alcoholism up close — in your father — and you're nothing like that. And at the same time... something happened that got your coach's attention.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, okay, my times have been off. And there was — [stops himself] look, I missed one practice. Once. And suddenly it's this whole intervention. But everyone else on the team goes out just as hard as I do. Nobody's making them sit in a therapist's office.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels really unfair to be singled out when you don't see yourself as doing anything different from your teammates. And at the same time, I'm hearing someone who clearly cares deeply about being on that team — even if things have gotten complicated lately.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do care. That's the thing that kills me. I've been on varsity since freshman year. I have worked — like, you don't even know — I've worked so hard to be here. My times are off because there's been a lot of other stuff going on too. It's not just... it's not only the drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A lot going on. Yeah... What does being on this team actually mean to you? Like, beyond just running — what does it give you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... [long pause] it's the only thing I've ever been really good at. My family doesn't have money. I'm here on scholarship. If I lose that... I don't — I genuinely don't know what happens. Track has been my whole life since I was like eight years old.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Track is who you are. It's not just a sport — it's where you came from, what got you here, and what you'd be putting at risk.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I know that. I'm not stupid — I know that when I'm out Thursday night and then I'm supposed to run Friday morning, it hurts me. I know that. I just... it's the only way I know how to turn my brain off. After a meet, after a bad day, after anything. I just — I don't know what else to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect a few things back, if that's okay. You came in today feeling pushed into this — which makes complete sense. And underneath that there's someone who has worked incredibly hard his whole life, who knows exactly what's at stake with this scholarship, who can see the connection between drinking and his performance, and who's also looking for a way to turn his brain off because he doesn't have another one yet. That's a lot to carry.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. [quiet] I don't know why it's so hard to just not do it. After the last meet I swore I wasn't gonna go out. Like I told myself. And then I was out by ten o'clock.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture where you want to be in a year — what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: On the team. Running. Like... actually running the times I know I'm capable of. I set a personal record sophomore year and I haven't even been close since then. I think about that a lot, actually. More than I let on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You haven't let go of that version of yourself — the one who ran that personal record. You're still holding onto him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't, no. [small laugh] I kind of thought coming here would be someone telling me what to do, like a lecture or whatever. But talking about the running actually makes me want to — I don't know. Try. Like, actually try this time, not just because coach is watching.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feels different — wanting it for yourself. What would trying look like for you this week? Just one small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not going out Thursday. Just this Thursday. That's always where it starts — Thursday nights. If I can get through one Thursday, I think I could actually run a decent practice Friday morning for once. Like, an actual one.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, have a seat. I know you mentioned you're a bit pressed for time today, so I appreciate you making it here. How are you doing this morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm... okay, I guess. It's fine. I mean, I didn't really have much choice about coming, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up. That matters, even when it doesn't feel like a choice. A lot of people in your situation just... don't. So tell me a little about what's been going on for you lately — not just the court stuff, but generally. How's life been since you retired?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's been... I don't know, weird. I thought retirement was gonna be great, you know? Like, all this freedom. But my wife passed two years ago, my kids are busy with their own lives, and I'm just... rattling around that house. I volunteered at the library for a bit but that kind of petered out. It's quiet. Really quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of quiet can be deafening. You went from a full life — work, your wife, a sense of purpose every day — and then all of that just... stopped. All at once, almost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And I know — I know people are gonna say, oh, the drinking, that's the problem, but I'm not... look, I'm not some alcoholic sitting in a gutter. I have a couple drinks in the evening. It helps me sleep. It's — it's not like I'm falling down drunk or whatever. The DUI thing, that was a one-time thing, I made a mistake, I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not minimizing what happened — you're owning that it was a mistake. That takes some honesty. And at the same time, you're telling me the drinking itself is serving a purpose. It's helping you get through the nights.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's exactly it. I mean, what am I supposed to do, just sit there staring at the walls? At least when I have a drink I feel a little... I don't know, relaxed. Like things are okay for a minute. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What else has changed since you started drinking more in the evenings? The doctor mentioned some things at your last visit — I'm wondering what your take is on all of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's... yeah, he flagged some liver numbers. Said they were elevated. And I — look, I know that's not great. I'm not an idiot. But I also think doctors can be a bit alarmist sometimes, you know? Like, one bad reading and suddenly it's a whole thing. I've been healthy my whole life. Worked hard, ate decent, never smoked. It just feels like... like I finally get to relax and now everyone's on my case.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've taken care of yourself for sixty-five years. You've earned that. And somewhere in there, part of you is worried — otherwise you wouldn't have mentioned the liver numbers at all.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. I am. I don't — I don't wanna die early, you know? Sandra, my wife, she went fast. Cancer. Didn't see it coming. And I keep thinking, what if I'm doing this to myself? What if I'm the one making myself sick? That thought scares me more than anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You watched someone you loved get taken without warning. And now you're sitting with the fear that you might be doing something that shortens the time you have. That's a heavy thing to carry around every night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. It really is. And — and my son, he has a kid now. My granddaughter, she's two. I barely know her. And I think about... I want to be around for that. I want her to know me. Not just some old man who died before she could remember him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to be present for her. Really present — not just alive, but someone she actually knows and remembers. What do you think gets in the way of that right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... the drinking, obviously. I know that. And just — the way I've been living, sort of shut off from everything. My son invites me to things and I usually say no because, I don't know, I'd rather just stay home. Which is... that's not great. I know that sounds bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound bad — it sounds like someone who's been grieving and coping the best way they knew how. Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You lost your wife, you lost your routine, and you've been lonely in a way that's hard to put into words. The drinking has helped you get through the nights, but you can see it's starting to cost you — your health, your relationship with your son and granddaughter, and honestly, the version of yourself you want to be. And something in you came here today — even if you had to — because some part of you is ready to think about what comes next.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I didn't expect you to — I don't know, I thought you were just gonna lecture me. But that's... that's exactly it. I don't want the next ten years to look like the last two. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Lecturing's not really my style. So — given everything you've just said — what feels like one small thing you could actually see yourself doing differently this week? Not a big overhaul, just one thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I could call my son. Actually call him, not just text. And maybe say yes next time he invites me for dinner. I don't know if I'm ready to quit drinking cold turkey or whatever, but I think — yeah. I could do that. That feels like something I can actually do.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come in, please... take your time, make yourself comfortable. There's no rush at all. I'm really glad you came in today. Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I saw something online, like a flyer or — I don't know, maybe an ad. And I just... I thought maybe I would come. I almost didn't, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like it took something real just to walk through that door today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I've never done anything like this before. I don't really... I mean, I'm not someone who talks about their problems. In my family we just — you deal with things yourself, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Talking about personal things doesn't really come naturally to you. And yet here you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I mean, my situation is a bit complicated. I moved here about two years ago. By myself. And things have just been — hard. I drink sometimes to help me sleep or just, like, unwind after work. It's not like I have a problem or anything, I just wanted to maybe talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two years in a new place, completely on your own... that's a lot to carry. And drinking has been one way of getting through those hard nights.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I didn't expect it to be this lonely, honestly. Back home I had my family — they were always around, my mom, my cousins. Friends from school. Here I go to work, I come home, that's it. Nobody calls to check on me. Sometimes I go a whole weekend without talking to a single person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A whole weekend without a single conversation. That kind of silence can be really painful. What does the drinking feel like, when those weekends get hard?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... it helps for a while. Like I'll pour a glass and put on something familiar on TV — something from home — and for a bit it feels okay. Less empty, I guess. But then I wake up at two in the morning and it's worse than before. And I've been drinking more than I used to. Like, I notice that. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you knows something has shifted — the amount has crept up, the relief doesn't really last. There's a part of you that's been paying quiet attention to that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... yeah. I've never actually said that out loud before. It's strange to say it. Like if I say it then it becomes real, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would you want to be different? If things could shift, even just a little — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to feel less alone. That's... I think that's the real thing. The drinking is just filling a hole, right? If I had people — if I had even one person here I could actually call — maybe I wouldn't need it so much. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's such a clear and honest thing to name. You've just put your finger on something really important — that the loneliness is at the heart of this for you. That takes a lot of self-awareness.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nobody ever said that to me. Like... nobody has ever actually told me that what I feel makes sense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing, if that's okay. You moved here alone, and two years in, the isolation has been much harder than you expected. Drinking became a way to cope — to make those quiet weekends feel a little less empty. And somewhere along the way you noticed it's gotten heavier, and it doesn't really fix the loneliness the way you hoped. What you're really longing for, underneath all of it, is connection. Someone to reach out to. Does that feel right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I didn't think someone would understand that so quickly. I thought you'd just tell me to stop drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you're here. What would feel like a small, manageable step — something that might help you start building even a little more of that connection you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... coming back here? I don't know. I feel like I could actually talk to you. I wasn't expecting to feel that today.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back. That took something — coming back after last week, when you weren't sure this was even worth it. Before we get into anything heavy, how are you feeling right now, walking in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... nervous, I guess. I almost didn't come. Sat in my car for like fifteen minutes out front. I don't know. I figured — I mean, I'm already here, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You almost didn't come, and you came anyway. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I don't feel like it's... I don't know, brave or whatever. I just — my wife basically said she'd leave if I didn't keep coming. So there's that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of what brought you through that door is wanting to keep your marriage. And I'm curious — is that the only reason? Or is there something else going on inside you that made you sit in that car and eventually walk in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I mean. The three years. I had three years. I was — I was at meetings, I had a sponsor, the whole thing. And I just... threw it away. Like it was nothing. And I can't stop thinking about that. Like what kind of person does that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The shame of it is eating at you. Three years of real work, and now you're looking at yourself and asking what that says about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And the thing is — it wasn't even like I was tempted for months or whatever. It was just... I got the call that I was laid off, and that night I was at a bar. Like it happened that fast. Twenty-two years at that company and they just... and I just...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. And then one phone call, and the ground disappeared. What was going through your mind in those hours between the call and the bar — do you remember?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Nothing. That's the thing. It was like... static. Like I just went numb and my body just sort of... went where it always used to go. I didn't even decide. I just ended up there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's like the old automatic pilot kicked in before you even had a chance to think. The grief and the shock were so overwhelming that the part of you that had three years of recovery — it just got bypassed completely.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... when you put it like that. I still feel like I should've — I knew better. I had all the tools. I'd been through hard stuff before sober. My dad died, I stayed sober through that. So why not this? Why was this different?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You stayed sober through losing your father. That's remarkable — that tells me something real about the kind of strength you've had. And you're also asking a really honest question right now, which is: what made this one different? What do you think it was?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My identity, maybe. I don't know. My dad dying was... terrible, but I still had my job. I still had a reason to get up. This felt like... like who I was just got erased. I was the guy who showed up, you know? For twenty-two years. That was me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You've told me that you came back today even though you almost didn't. That you're still thinking about those three years, not as something lost, but as something that meant something to you. That you understand, at least partly, what happened — this wasn't weakness, it was a profound loss of identity happening in an instant. And you stayed sober through your father's death, which tells me the capacity is still in you. That's a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I hadn't thought about it like that. I keep just beating myself up. I haven't been back to AA because I can't look those guys in the eye. But I used to... I used to really believe in that stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You used to really believe in it. What would it mean to you if you could walk back into a meeting?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think it would mean... I was still that person. The one who was trying. Not — not the guy I've been for the last three months. I'm so tired of being that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're tired of being that guy. And somewhere underneath all the shame, you still know who you want to be. That's not nothing — that's actually where change starts. So before we close today, I'd like to ask: what's one small thing — not a big commitment, just one thing — that might feel like a step toward the person you're describing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... texting my old sponsor. I haven't talked to him since it happened. I've been too ashamed. But he'd — he wouldn't judge me. He never did. Yeah. Maybe that.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it's not always easy to walk through that door for the first time. Make yourself comfortable — can I get you some water or anything before we get started?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nah, I'm good. Look, I'll be straight with you — I'm only here because my wife wouldn't let it go. Doctor says my liver numbers are 'elevated' or whatever, and now suddenly everyone's acting like I'm some kind of alcoholic. I'm not. I work construction, I've been doing it twenty years. A few beers after work is just... that's just what you do. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the people around you — your wife, your doctor — are pretty worried right now. I'm curious, setting all that aside for a moment... when you think about your drinking yourself, what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Nothing. Nothing comes up. I work ten, twelve hour days sometimes — on my feet, lifting, hauling, all of it. I come home, I have a few beers, I relax. That's it. I'm not sitting in a gutter somewhere. I show up to work every single day, I pay my bills, I take care of my family. So I don't... I don't see what the problem is. The doctor's probably just covering his ass, you know? Liability. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You work incredibly hard. Long days, physical labor. And those beers are how you come down from all of that. And you see yourself as someone who shows up — for work, for your family.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I mean... yeah. That's right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And when the doctor sat you down and told you about those liver tests — what was that like to hear?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Annoying, honestly. He's sitting there looking at me over his glasses going 'your ALT levels are elevated, you need to cut back significantly.' And I'm thinking — dude, I'm forty-two. I've been drinking since I was like seventeen. If there was really a problem, wouldn't it have shown up before now? So I just... I think he's being dramatic. That's all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you heard that and thought — this can't really be serious, I've been fine for years. And at the same time... you're here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I don't know. My wife cried. She actually cried when I told her about the tests. And that kind of... I don't know. That got to me a little. She doesn't cry easy, my wife.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seeing her that upset hit different than the doctor's words did. What do you think it is that she's scared of?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, she just — she worries too much, that's her thing. Always has. She worries about the kids, about money, about me. I keep telling her I'm fine, but she won't hear it. She found this place online and basically... look, I love my wife. But she kind of pushed me into coming here. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came here for her. Because you love her. Even if a big part of you isn't convinced there's something to worry about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean — look, I don't know. Maybe I drink a little more than most guys. I'm not gonna sit here and pretend otherwise. But it's never caused me real problems. Never. It's just... those liver numbers, I looked them up after the appointment. I didn't tell my wife I did that. But what I read... it wasn't great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something — looking that up, sitting with what you found. Even keeping it to yourself. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've got kids. Two of them — fourteen and eleven. And I don't... I want to be around, you know? I want to be at their graduations and all that stuff. I'm not trying to be stupid about this. It's just... the beer is how I relax. It's how I unwind. I don't know what I'd do without it after a day like today, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm following you — you work hard, the drinking helps you decompress, and it's been part of your life for a long time. You came in today partly because your wife was scared, and partly because something you read gave you pause. You're not ready to call this a problem exactly. And at the same time, you're thinking about your kids, about being there for them — and there's a part of you that's asking some questions maybe you haven't let yourself ask out loud before now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's pretty much it. I mean when you say it like that it sounds like — yeah. My dad, he drank a lot. He wasn't always... he wasn't always there. And I swore I'd be different. And I am, I'm nothing like him. But... I don't know. Sometimes I wonder if I'm kidding myself a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you've shared today — thinking about your kids, what you found when you looked up those numbers, what you just said about your dad — where do you think you'd want to go from here? What feels like a step that makes sense to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe — maybe I could just try cutting back. See how it goes. Not quit or anything, I'm not saying that, but... maybe not six every night. Maybe like three. See if I feel different. I think... I think I could actually try that.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. I'll be honest — a lot of people don't come back after the first session, so the fact that you're here says something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. My therapist basically wouldn't drop it. I'm not — I mean, I don't think I actually have a problem, I just figured it'd get her off my back if I came again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because someone else wanted you to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pretty much. I mean — look, I work full time, I have two kids, I do everything by myself. If I pour a glass of wine at the end of the day, that's... I don't know, that's just life. That's not a problem. That's surviving.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what a typical Tuesday night looks like for you. Like, walk me through it — from the time you pick the kids up to when you finally sit down.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh god. Um... okay so I leave work at five, I pick up Maya from her after-school thing, then I have to get Dominic from his dad's — which is always a whole thing — then it's dinner, which nobody wants to eat, then homework, then Maya's meltdown about something, then baths, then getting them to actually stay in bed... and by the time they're asleep it's like nine-thirty and I'm just... done. I'm completely done. So yeah. I open a bottle of wine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's an enormous amount to carry every single day. And that bottle of wine at nine-thirty — it sounds like it's the first moment in the whole day that's actually just yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. Like everything else is for someone else. That's the one thing that's — I don't know. Mine. It's quiet and it's mine and it makes the noise in my head stop for a little while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something really demanding — raising two kids on your own, holding down a job, managing everything. That takes a kind of strength most people don't even have to find out if they have.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel strong. I feel like I'm just... white-knuckling it most of the time. Like if one more thing goes wrong I'm going to completely fall apart. And I can't fall apart. They need me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does the wine actually do for you that nothing else has been able to do?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It just... turns the volume down. Like everything's screaming at me all day and then I have a glass and it's like someone turns a dial. I tried, like, baths and whatever, meditation or whatever people say. It doesn't work like that. The wine actually works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It works. And somewhere underneath that, I'm hearing something else — like you already know a bottle a night is more than turning the volume down.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Last week Maya asked me why I always have my special cup. She's seven. She called it my special cup. And I just — I laughed it off, I said it was grown-up juice, but afterward I went to the bathroom and I just stood there. I don't know. I don't want her to remember me that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What went through your mind standing in that bathroom?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My mom drank. I swore I would never — I mean, it wasn't like, bad bad. But I always knew. Kids always know. And I'm standing there thinking, am I doing the same thing? Am I becoming her? Because I really, really don't want to be doing that to them without even realizing it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think there's a lot here. You're exhausted in a way that's bone-deep — every day, for years, with no real break. The wine is the one thing that makes that bearable, and it actually works. And at the same time, Maya's comment cracked something open, because you grew up in a house where drinking was part of the wallpaper, and you've always been determined not to pass that on. Both of those things are true at the same time for you right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's — yeah. I didn't really think about it like that but... that's basically it. I'm not ready to like, quit or whatever. I don't even know if I could. But I don't want to be the mom with the special cup either. I don't know how to do both of those things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to figure that out today. But I'm curious — if things looked even a little different six months from now, what would you want that to look like? Just for you, not for anyone else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd want to not need it. Like I want to be able to sit in my house at night and just... be okay. Not have to pour something to feel okay. I want that to just be normal again. I don't know if it can be, but... I think that's what I want.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you again, Harold. How have things been going since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, um... not great, if I'm being honest with you. Had a rough week. I, uh... I drank more than I should have. Which I know. I know that's not... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being really honest with yourself about that. Something made this week harder than the others.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, it's... the house is just so quiet. You know? I keep thinking I should call someone, but who am I gonna call? My wife's been gone three years now. Most of my old work buddies have scattered. So I just... sit there. And I pour a glass, and at least it feels like something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking becomes a kind of company when the silence gets too loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah, that's it exactly. I had a routine for 38 years. Get up, go to the plant, people needed me to do my job right. Now I wake up and there's nothing. Nowhere to be. I was a machinist — I made things. Now I just... I don't make anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That loss — of work, of routine, of feeling needed — it sounds like it's sitting very heavy on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor told me my liver numbers are bad. Said I need to cut way back or there'll be consequences. And my daughter... she worries. But honestly? Sometimes I think... at 65, sitting alone in that house every day... what am I even cutting back for. What's the point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is asking whether there's still enough to live for to make the struggle worth it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to think that way, I really don't. But some mornings it just... washes over me. Like why am I doing this. Who even cares.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet — you kept coming back here on your own. You drove yourself today. That tells me something about you, Harold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter brought me the first time. The rest of them... I drove myself. I don't know why exactly. I guess some part of me isn't ready to just... give up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Some part of you is still fighting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She has two little kids. My grandkids — Mia's seven and the little one, Danny, he just turned four. And when I'm with them... that's the only time I feel like myself anymore. I don't want to miss watching them grow up because I drank myself into a hospital bed. I just... I couldn't live with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing. You've had a hard week — the loneliness hit you hard, the quiet house, losing that sense of purpose that work used to give you. Part of you wondered this week if it was even worth making changes. But then there's Mia and Danny. And there's the part of you that has been driving yourself here, week after week, without anyone making you. Those two things are still alive in you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. I guess I haven't completely given up. Maybe... maybe it's not too late. I'm only 65, right? My dad lived to 82.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thinking about the time you still have ahead — what feels like one small thing you might want to try differently this coming week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's a, um... there's a woodworking group at the senior center. I walked past the flyer like three times and just kept walking. Maybe I call them. Just to ask. I used to be real good with my hands.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A machinist who's good with his hands, thinking about making something again. That sounds like Harold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah. Maybe it is. I'll call them. And I'll... I'll try to keep it to one glass this week. Just one. I can do one.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. Welcome. I'm glad you made it — seriously, right after finishing detox, that's not nothing. So I want to hear it from you: what brought you in today? What made you set this up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My buddy basically dragged me. I did the detox thing, I checked the box, and now everyone's acting like I need to keep going to stuff. I'm not — look, I'm not some guy who, like, crashed a car or anything. I pour drinks for a living. This is just... kind of what that world is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is like — I did the hard part already, what more do people want from me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And the detox was — okay it was awful, I'll give it that. The shaking, not sleeping, all of it. But I got through it and I showed up to work and I'm fine. It's not like I'm some... I don't know. I'm functional. That should count for something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You pushed through something genuinely brutal and you're still standing — that matters. I hear you on the functional thing, I do. I'm curious though, and you don't have to have an answer — was there a moment, something just for you, not your buddy, not anyone else, where something felt off?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe. A few weeks back I was just sitting there and I tried to think of when I last had a sober day. Like just one. And I sat there for — I don't know, it felt like forever — and I couldn't come up with anything. Not one day. That was... yeah, that was kind of a weird feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Coming up completely blank on that — that unsettled you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I don't want to be dramatic about it. I'm 27, it's not — my dad didn't get his first DUI until he was like 40 so technically I'm way ahead of schedule, right? Ha. I don't know why I said that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Way ahead of schedule — okay, I'll take the dark humor, I appreciate it. But you said you don't know why you brought him up. What do you think? Why did your dad come to mind just now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because... I've been thinking about him more lately. Things didn't go well for him. Like, really didn't. And I keep telling myself I'm different, but then I look at my week and it's just — work, drink, sleep, work, drink, sleep — and it's like... I don't know. It looks familiar. In a bad way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see the pattern laid out in front of you, and there's a part of you going, 'I've seen this movie before.' That's a hard thing to sit with. And honest.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want his life. I really don't. I love the guy but his world got... small. Like really small. And I've got — I had things I wanted to do. I was supposed to go to culinary school. I still think about that sometimes, which is probably pathetic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not pathetic at all. Culinary school — tell me more about that. What did that life look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wanted to open my own place. An actual restaurant, not just a bar. And I can cook — like genuinely, I'm good at it. But I started bartending for cash when I was 22 and then just... stayed. And now every shift I'm surrounded by bottles and I go home and open one because I don't know what else to do with myself. But the restaurant thing — I don't know. Maybe it's too late. I'm already 27.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: 27 is not too late for culinary school. I feel like I need to just say that out loud. And the fact that you're still carrying that dream — it didn't go anywhere. There's something alive in there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's been a while since I said it out loud. It feels less stupid saying it here than it does in my head at 2am. I guess I'm scared I've already messed up too much to actually go after it. Like, what if I get there and I can't hack it because I... because of all this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I reflect back what I've heard, because I think you've said some really significant things today? You came in not totally sold on being here — fair. But you also just got through detox, which is genuinely hard. You had that moment where you couldn't find a single sober day and it shook you. You don't want to follow your dad's path. And there's this version of yourself — with a restaurant, doing something real — that you haven't let go of. That's a lot of things pointing the same direction.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. When you lay it out like that... I've been trying not to look at all of it at once because it's a lot to look at. But yeah. It's all there. It's been there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is a lot. And you don't have to sort all of it out today — that's literally what this is for. But I want to ask you one thing. Given everything you just said... what's one thing, just one, you'd want to be different a year from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to actually have days off. Like, real ones I can remember. And... maybe sign up for one class. Just one. I know that's not — that's not a big thing, but. That could be a start, right?

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm glad you found us — the website can be a bit of a maze, honestly. I keep telling them to fix it but, you know, bureaucracy. Make yourself comfortable. Can I get you some water or anything before we get started?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, no, I'm good. Thanks. Um... yeah, I've never actually done this before, so I'm not really sure how it works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's totally fair — most people walking through that door for the first time feel exactly that way. There's no script here, no checklist I'm running through. Basically, this is your time. So I guess the best place to start is just... what made today the day you came in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, so... I mean, I've been in a PhD program for about two years now and it's like — okay, I know everyone says grad school is stressful, right, that's just the deal — but lately I've kind of been using alcohol to, like, take the edge off? And it started as just a glass of wine after a long day and now I'm looking at my week and it's... more than that. I found some stuff online about, I don't know, how that can become a pattern, and I figured I should probably talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it started as something that felt manageable — just a way to decompress — and somewhere along the way you noticed the volume had kind of... crept up on you. And that caught your attention enough to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And it's not like I'm — I don't wake up craving it or anything. It's more like... the moment my laptop closes at night, my brain is still just running, you know? All this stuff about my dissertation, whether my ideas are even good, whether I actually belong in this program at all. And the drinking is like... it turns that down. But then I wake up the next morning feeling kind of foggy and I've lost half the morning and I'm already behind and that makes the anxiety worse and then — yeah. It's a loop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That loop sounds exhausting. I want to make sure I'm understanding the day-to-day of it — what does a typical week actually look like for you, in terms of drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly probably five, six nights a week? It's usually at home, not like going out to bars or whatever — so it doesn't feel like a big deal in that sense. It's just like three or four drinks while I'm trying to wind down. I know that's... I mean, I know that's not nothing. But I'm still showing up to my meetings, I'm still producing work, it's just — the work isn't as sharp as it used to be. I can tell. My advisor mentioned something last week and that kind of... stuck.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to pause on something, because I think it's actually pretty significant — you noticed it yourself before your advisor said anything. That takes a kind of honesty with yourself that not everyone has, especially when things are already stressful. What did your advisor say, if you don't mind me asking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said my last draft felt... unfocused. Like I was just sort of going through the motions. And she asked if everything was okay, kind of gently, and I said yeah, just tired. But sitting there I was like — I know exactly why it's unfocused. And I couldn't say that. That was a really uncomfortable moment.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like it hit different than you expected. What worries you most about what she said — or about where this is heading if nothing changes?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... losing the PhD. That's — that's the big one. I've wanted to do this research since undergrad. I turned down a job offer that was paying real money to do this. And the idea that I could just, like, drink my way out of the thing I actually care about most... that's terrifying. That's genuinely terrifying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking started as a way to cope with the pressure of something you care deeply about — and now it's become a threat to that very thing. That's a really painful contradiction to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I never framed it that way but that's — huh. I came into this program because I genuinely believe the research I'm doing matters. And I'm like sabotaging it to survive the day-to-day stress of doing it. That doesn't make any sense when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure I've got it right. You came in today on your own — no one made you — because you've been watching a coping strategy quietly get bigger than you wanted it to be. You notice the fog, you notice the drop in your work quality, and your advisor's comment confirmed what you already suspected. And underneath all of it is this research that you actually sacrificed for, that you genuinely believe in. It sounds like part of you is saying: this isn't who I want to be in this program.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It's not. I didn't move across the country and give up a real salary to be the guy who drinks alone every night and turns in foggy drafts. That's... no. That's not — I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You clearly know something needs to shift. What would it actually look like — in your day, in your week — if you got a handle on this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... waking up and actually feeling rested. Like, having that first hour of the morning where my brain is actually on and I'm reading and thinking clearly and not just playing catch-up. I used to have that. First year I had that. And writing — writing felt good when I wasn't running on fumes. I want that back. I think I could get that back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here not knowing what to expect, you've never done this before, and in one conversation you've named the loop, connected it to something that genuinely matters to you, and you can already picture what it looks like on the other side. That's not nothing. That's actually a really solid place to start working from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I think I've kind of known for a while that I needed to do something. I just didn't know if talking about it would actually help. But this... yeah, okay. I'm glad I came in.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... you made it in today. That took something, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. What's going through your head as you sit here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think this whole thing is ridiculous. My doctor flagged some liver numbers and now everyone's acting like I'm some kind of alcoholic. I'm twenty-one. I go out on weekends. That's literally what college is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting, this reaction — your doctor, your parents, the intervention — it all feels way overblown for what you see as pretty normal behavior.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Like, my whole friend group does the same stuff. Nobody's dragging them in to see a therapist. It just feels like I'm being singled out for — I don't know — for being a normal college guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about those lab results. What did the doctor actually say to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said my — whatever — my liver enzymes were elevated. Which, I looked it up, and that can happen from like, tons of stuff. Ibuprofen. A stomach bug. She just automatically assumed it was drinking because she saw it on my chart. It's like she'd already made up her mind before I even walked in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You did your homework — went and looked it up instead of just taking her word for it. That tells me you're someone who thinks for himself. And I'm also curious: when you first saw those numbers, before you started Googling, what was the very first thing you felt?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I was annoyed. Mostly. Like, great, another thing to deal with. But it wasn't like I was scared or whatever. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean — for you, your life — if the doctor was right? Not saying she is. Just... what if she was?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's not — I mean, that's a pretty hypothetical question. She's not right. I went through that detox program, which was a complete waste of two weeks of my semester, by the way, and I feel completely fine. I feel great, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel great. And also you lost two weeks of your semester. And your friends staged an intervention. And your liver numbers came back flagged. I'm just putting back what you've told me — that's a lot of things piling up at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
