utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds way worse than it is. Those things aren't — they're not connected. The intervention was my roommate being dramatic, the detox was my parents overreacting, and the labs are probably nothing. Stop lumping it all together like it's some big pattern, because it's not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at just one piece then. The detox — what was that actually like for you, being in there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I don't know. Uncomfortable. They monitor you the whole time and I had some — my hands were shaking the first couple days, which they said was normal, but it didn't feel normal. And I couldn't sleep at all. But that's just what happens when you stop drinking suddenly. That's a medical withdrawal thing. It's not about being, like, an addict.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Shaking hands. Not sleeping. You got through something genuinely hard and you're still here. I want to make sure I'm hearing you right though — you're telling me it was withdrawal, a medical process, you know what caused it. You're not calling yourself an addict. And what you just described is your body physically depending on alcohol to function.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I know what physical dependence is. I'm not an idiot. It doesn't mean — look, plenty of people drink heavily and stop and have symptoms. That's just chemistry. That doesn't automatically make them alcoholics. Words matter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Words do matter. You're right. And I notice you know a lot — about withdrawal, about dependence, about the difference between physical and psychological. I'm not here to put a label on you. That's not what this is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Because that's what everyone else seems to be trying to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like for you to walk out of here today feeling like this wasn't a complete waste of your time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... don't know. Maybe just — not having everyone on my back for five seconds. I'm not saying I want to change everything. I'm just saying I'm tired of feeling like I'm constantly on trial.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today, especially with a busy schedule. I know you mentioned you're between classes, so I want to make sure we use this time in a way that's actually useful for you. Can you tell me a little about what brought you in — in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... my manager kind of made it a thing. Like, there was this situation at work last week and he said I had to come talk to someone or — I don't know, it was pretty clear it wasn't optional. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it wasn't entirely your choice to be here, and yet you showed up anyway. That says something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say here. I'm a bartender. I drink. That's kind of — that's the job, you know? Everyone I work with does it. You close down, you have a couple drinks, you wind down. It's not like I'm showing up hammered or whatever. It was just one bad night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking after a shift is just part of the culture, part of how you decompress. And at the same time, something happened that was significant enough that your manager felt he needed to act. What was going through your mind when that happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I barely remember it. Like, that's the thing. I remember starting my shift, and then — there are just gaps. And I know that sounds bad. It sounds really bad saying it out loud. I'd had a rough few days and I think I... I think I'd been drinking before I even got there. Which I've never — I mean, I've done it but not like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took courage to say. The gaps, drinking before work — you're describing something that clearly scared you a little.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, it did. It does. I sat in my car after and I was like, when did this become — I tried to think of the last day I didn't drink and I couldn't. I genuinely could not think of one. And that felt... I don't know. Empty, kind of. Like something was wrong with the math.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Empty. Like the numbers didn't add up to the person you thought you were.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. I'm not — I'm not some like, sad alcoholic at a bar, you know? That's not me. I've got school, I've got plans. I wanted to open my own place someday. But lately it's like... I don't know, I'm tired all the time and I'm not working on any of that stuff. I just work, drink, sleep, work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still have that vision — your own place, a real future — and right now there's this gap between that person and where you're at day to day. What does that feel like to sit with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. It feels awful. Like... what if I already messed it up? What if this is already who I am now and I just didn't notice it happening? I'm 27. My dad was — he had a problem. I swore I wasn't going to be that. And now I'm sitting here and I'm like... I don't know. Maybe it doesn't matter what you swear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying your father's story alongside your own this whole time. And the fact that you're making that connection — that you're sitting here asking these questions at 27 — that's actually different from what you described about him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He never would've come somewhere like this. He thought — he thought asking for help was weak. So I guess... yeah. Maybe that's something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in because you had to, but somewhere in this conversation you've talked about gaps in your memory that frightened you, not being able to recall a sober day, losing ground on your own goals, and a fear that you might be repeating a pattern you promised yourself you'd break. That's a lot to hold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it all together like that it's... yeah. It's heavier than I let myself think about normally. I kind of just — I stay in the moment. Don't look too far ahead or too far back. But when you line it all up...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Staying in the moment has been a way of getting through. And now part of you is wondering if it's also been a way of not seeing the full picture. If things were different — if you felt like you had some real control back — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'd wake up not feeling like garbage. I'd maybe actually open that business plan document I've had sitting there for like eight months. I'd call my sister back, she's been — she's been worried. I keep blowing her off. I don't know, just like... feeling like I'm moving somewhere instead of just spinning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That picture you just painted — waking up clear, working on something that matters, reconnecting with your sister — that's not small. That's the life you actually want. And you came in here today, which means some part of you is already moving toward it. I'd like to keep talking, if you're open to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I am.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in... take whatever seat feels comfortable. I'm glad you made it. I know walk-in sessions can feel a little disorienting — you're not sure what to expect, you don't know who you're walking into. So I just want to ask, before we do anything else — what would feel most useful for you today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. I mean... I was told I had to be here. By the court. So. I don't really — I'm not sure I have an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because someone else said you had to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. There was an... incident. In the parking lot. At my kids' school, which I know — I know how that sounds. I'm not that person. I want to be clear about that. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. And I'm not here to make you into a version of yourself you don't recognize. I'm curious about who you actually are. What does your life look like right now — like on a regular Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have two kids. Eight and eleven. Their dad's been gone three years — not gone gone, just... not here. I work full time at a property management office. I do homework, I do dinner, I do bedtime, I do... all of it. By myself. Every day. I don't know what else you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You are holding an enormous amount. And you walked in here today on top of all of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't exactly have a choice. [pause] But... yeah. It's a lot. It's been a lot for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does the end of the day look like for you — once the kids are in bed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I sit down. I pour a glass of wine. And I just... I sit there. Sometimes I pour another. By the end of the night the bottle's gone. I know that's — I know. Okay? I already know what you're going to say and I know it's too much. I'm not stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you already knows it's more than you want it to be. And at the same time... that hour after they're asleep, that's the one moment in the day that belongs to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's the only time I'm not somebody's mom or somebody's employee or somebody who's behind on something. It's just... quiet. I don't know how to explain it. It's like the noise just stops.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That quiet. That hour where the noise stops and you can just... exist without needing to be anything. I hear how much you need that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter asked me last week why I smell like that in the morning. She's eight. She wasn't even — she wasn't mad, she was just asking, like it was a normal question. [voice tightens] And I just made her breakfast. I didn't say anything. I just made her eggs and didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] I don't want her to grow up and think that's who her mom was. That's not... I had a mom like that, and I swore I would never — [stops herself] I just don't know when it turned into this. I don't know when it got away from me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You came in today because you had to — that's real, and there's no pretending otherwise. But underneath that, there's a woman who has been carrying everything, alone, for years. Who found something that made the noise stop. And who is now sitting here, thinking about her daughter's face at the breakfast table, and wondering if the thing that was holding her together might be pulling something else apart. Does that feel close to where you are?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quietly] Yeah. [pause] That's... yeah. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Setting aside the court, setting aside what anyone else needs from you right now — when you imagine what your life could look like, what you actually want it to look like... what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to remember putting her to bed. Like actually remember it. I want to wake up and not feel like garbage before the day even starts. I want to be... I don't know. I used to be okay. I was okay before. I just want to feel like that again.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. ... I want to say, that matters. Coming back when it's hard — that takes something. So... what's been sitting with you this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I kept... I found myself thinking about what you said. About the art. I wasn't sure I'd come back, honestly. But here I am, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. ... Something pulled you back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I've been noticing things. Little things. Like, I painted something last weekend and I just... I looked at it and felt nothing. Like it could've been anyone's work. Not mine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a painful thing to feel about your own work. I'm curious — you've told me that drinking is part of how you create, that it helps you access something real. What does that look like, when it's working the way you want it to?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... okay, so when I have a couple glasses, I stop censoring myself, you know? Like the inner critic just shuts up. And I can just — I used to just go. The work would pour out. I'm scared that without it I'd just... nothing. That I'd sit there with a blank canvas and have absolutely nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The alcohol silences the critic. And under that silence, something real used to come through. And now you're scared that if you take it away... that critic comes back, and louder. And maybe there's nothing underneath it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. What if that's all I am without it? What if... what if the drinking isn't even the problem? What if I'm the problem, and the drinking was just — hiding it this whole time?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really vulnerable thing to say. ... Can you tell me more about what you actually see when you look at your recent work? What's there, versus what you hoped would be there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's flat. Like — technically it's fine, I guess. The lines are fine. But there's nothing alive in it. I used to feel something looking at my own work. Pride, or even just... recognition. Like, yes, that's me, that came from me. And now it's like I'm painting through glass. I can see the shape of what I'm trying to do but I can't actually reach it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Painting through glass. ... You can see yourself there, but you can't quite touch it. You're grieving something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I think I am. I've been — god, I've been drinking to get back to a place I used to just... live in. And every time I think, this time, this glass, this night. And then I look at what I made and it's just... it's not there. It hasn't been there for a while. I don't know when I stopped being me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of this for a moment. You came back today because something wouldn't let you go. You're noticing the work feels hollow — that you're working harder, drinking more to find that place, and it keeps pulling further away. And underneath all of that is this fear: that the creativity isn't really yours. That it belongs to the alcohol. ... That's a lot to carry around.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... I mean, yeah. It's exhausting. I didn't realize how much I've been chasing something. And I'm so tired. Like, I'm genuinely so tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you something, and take your time with it. Before the daily drinking became what it is now — before it was every night — what was creating like for you then? Where did the work come from?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... I was angrier then. More unsettled. But honestly? The work was better. I was broke and kind of a mess but I was making things I actually believed in. I think I started drinking more when things got stable. Like, I got afraid of the mess. Afraid of actually needing something and not having it. The drinking kind of... smoothed it all out. And the work got smooth too, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The creativity was always yours. It came from the unsettled place, the mess, the fear — not from the alcohol. The alcohol maybe felt like it gave you permission to go back there. But that place... it was you. It's always been you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it that way. I've been so convinced that I needed it to... function, to create. But maybe I just needed permission. Maybe I've been so scared of myself, of what comes up when I'm not numbing it, that I never let myself find out. ... That's terrifying. But it also kind of feels like — I don't know. Like maybe that's something I can actually work with?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today not even sure you were coming back. And somewhere in this conversation you found your way to the real question — not whether alcohol helps you create, but what you're afraid to feel without it. That took real courage. And what you just said — 'maybe that's something I can work with' — I don't want that to slip past us. That was you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've spent like six years — six years — thinking I was protecting my art. And maybe I've just been protecting my fear. I want to find out what I can actually do on my own. Like, I genuinely want to know that now.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm glad you made it — I know parking around here is basically a contact sport. So, I got a little background from the referral, but I'd rather hear it from you. What's been going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, the parking is... yeah. Um. I don't really know where to start, honestly. My supervisor kind of suggested I talk to someone. I've been — I work ER, twelve-hour shifts, and it's been... a lot. Since COVID, really. I mean, it was bad before but then it just... I don't know. I started having a drink or two after shifts to wind down and I guess that became more of a thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A drink or two to wind down — and somewhere along the way that shifted into something that's harder to ignore. What does that look like for you now, like on a typical night after a shift?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... okay so I get home, usually like two or three in the morning, and my brain just won't stop. Like I'll be in my kitchen and I'm still seeing the faces from the shift, you know? The stuff that didn't go well. And I know the wine helps me actually — like, get to sleep. So it started as two glasses and now it's... more. But I'm not like, drinking at work or anything. I want to be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's really important that you said that — and I hear you, this isn't about work performance, it's about what happens after. The shift ends but your nervous system hasn't gotten the memo. The images stick around.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And nobody — people who aren't in healthcare don't get it. I had a patient code three times in one night last month. Three times. And then I drove home and my roommate's watching Netflix and eating cereal and I'm just... I can't just be normal after that. The wine is the only thing that like, puts a wall up between me and all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying things that most people will never see, and you've basically had to figure out on your own how to survive it. That's not weakness — that's someone doing what they could with what they had. I'm also noticing something, though. You mentioned faces. Stuff that didn't go well. Sounds like this isn't just stress — it's more like the weight of what you've witnessed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, it is. I used to be able to compartmentalize really well. That was like my whole thing. My coworkers would always say, oh Sarah's unflappable. And now I just... I don't know. I feel like I lost that. And I feel guilty too because I know what alcohol does to people. I'm a nurse. I know the liver panels, I know the withdrawal stuff, I know all of it. And I'm still doing it. That's — I don't know what that says about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It says you're human. And honestly? Sometimes knowing exactly what's happening and still feeling like you can't stop — that's one of the more painful versions of this. The guilt gets layered on top of everything else. What do you think you've lost most, since all this ramped up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My mornings. I used to go running. Like, I was a runner. 5Ks, I was training for a half-marathon before COVID. Now I wake up feeling like garbage and the thought of running is... and I've gained weight and I just don't recognize myself a little bit. And I called in last week. Which I never do. I never call in. I was that person who came in sick and got everyone else sick, you know? Last week I called in because I was too hungover.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one landed differently when you said it — I could hear it. Calling in. For someone who showed up sick, that was a line.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It really was. And I — yeah. My team needed me and I wasn't there because of something I did to myself. That's different. That's not the pandemic's fault, that's not my supervisor's fault, that's... that's me. And I don't like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think there's a lot here. You came in today because your supervisor suggested it — not exactly your idea. But in the last twenty minutes you've talked about losing your mornings, losing the runner you used to be, feeling guilty because you know the clinical reality, and now this moment last week where you weren't there for your team. That's not someone who doesn't care. That's someone who cares a lot and is really tired.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I am so tired. I'm tired of being tired. I thought I was protecting myself, you know, with the drinking, and maybe I was for a while but now it's like... the thing I was using to cope is also making things worse and I can't — I don't know how to stop without losing the only thing that makes me feel okay after a shift.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named something really important — there's a real function it's been serving. The alcohol isn't random, it's been doing a job. Helping you get some distance from brutal shifts. The question isn't how do you just stop — it's what else could do that job, or part of that job, without the costs you're paying now. What have you tried, even small things, that helped even a little?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Running used to do it. Like after a bad shift I'd just... go. Even at weird hours. That worked. And sometimes calling my sister, she's also in healthcare so she gets it. But I stopped doing both of those. I don't really know why. It's like when you're in it, the easiest thing is just the wine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know what works for you. That's actually huge — some people spend months figuring that out. The running, the sister who speaks ER. Those didn't stop working, you just got too depleted to reach for them. What would it take to make one of those easier to reach than the bottle, even once this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... text my sister before I even get in my car after a shift. Like, preemptive. So I'm already in a conversation with someone instead of just driving home in silence and then opening the fridge. That might actually — yeah. That could work. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I love that plan because it's yours — I didn't hand it to you. You thought of it. And it uses something that's already real: your sister, your relationship, a system that worked. That's a solid place to start. I also want to say — you came in here today pretty guarded, and I get that, this isn't exactly a comfortable thing to do. But you didn't stay guarded. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I didn't really want to be here, I'll be honest. But this was — it wasn't what I expected. I thought it would be more like, here's a pamphlet, you have a drinking problem, go to AA. This felt more like... I don't know. Like I could actually figure something out. Which I haven't felt in a while.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Last time we talked, things were starting to feel a little different for you. How's the week been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. Look, I'm only here because my wife basically said I had to be. I don't — I don't think I need to be sitting here talking about this stuff every week. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is wondering what the point of all this really is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not just wondering. Like — back in the unit, everybody drank. That was just... that's what you do. You come home, you crack a beer, you decompress. Nobody was shipping anybody off to therapy over it. It was just normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That was part of the culture — the way things got done after a long day or a hard op.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And now suddenly I'm the problem? Because my wife decides she doesn't like it? My buddies drink way more than me. Nobody's dragging them into an office somewhere. So what is this, seriously.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like you're being singled out. Like the rules changed on you and nobody gave you the memo.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. I mean — I served for nine years. Nine years. And I come back and I can't even have a few drinks without... I don't know. It's like nothing I did over there counts anymore and now I'm just, what, some drunk who needs to be fixed? That's what I am now?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nine years is a long time to carry what you carried. That kind of thing doesn't just clock out when you do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It doesn't. It really doesn't. And — okay, fine. Maybe I drink more than I used to. I'll give you that. But it... it helps. It shuts everything off for a few hours. I can actually sleep. You know how long it's been since I slept a full night without it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking is doing something real for you. It's not nothing — it's giving you relief from something that's still very much there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And I... look, I know Sarah's upset. My wife. She's not — she's not wrong to be upset, I get that part. I just don't know what she expects me to do. Just stop and then everything's magically fine? It doesn't work like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even when all of this is making you angry, Sarah keeps coming up. She's still... somewhere in the middle of it for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's... yeah. She is. She's actually the reason I came back in one piece, if I'm being honest. We were solid before I deployed. Really solid. And now I can see her trying — like she's still trying — and I just keep... I don't know. I keep messing it up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I've got this right. Nine years of stuff that doesn't just go away. Drinking that actually works for something — the sleep, the quiet in your head. And at the same time, Sarah's still someone you're fighting to hold onto, even when you're not sure how. That sound close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I had a rough week. Drank more than I planned to. And she brought up the D word again. Divorce. And I usually just get pissed when she says it, but this time it... it hit different. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was different about it this time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Usually when she says it I just... I get angry, right, I shut down. But this time I actually looked at her. And she wasn't angry. She was just... tired. And sad. And I thought — I'm doing this. Not the Army. Not what happened over there. Me. I'm the one making her look like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when you really saw her. The drinking stopped being just your thing to manage. It became something happening to her too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't know what to do with it yet. I'm not gonna sit here and tell you I've got some plan. But I can't lose her. That's the one thing I'm actually sure of right now.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey... come on in. I'm really glad you made it today. I know this week was a rough one.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I didn't exactly have a choice, did I? Court says I show up, so I show up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't feel like your choice, being here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not. None of this is. I got one DUI — one — and now I'm sitting here every week like I'm some kind of... I don't know. Problem drinker. I'm a good mom. My kids are taken care of. Always.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want me to understand that. That being a good mom — that's at the center of who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do everything by myself. Full-time job, school pickups, homework, dinners, bath time, appointments — nobody helps me. Nobody. So yeah, I pour a glass of wine when they're in bed. Maybe more than one. That's not a crime. Or it — it shouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been running on empty for a long time with no one to hand things off to. And the wine — it sounds like it was the one thing that was just yours. Your way to finally breathe at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. That's exactly it. And now everyone acts like I'm some kind of monster and I'm — I'm not. I just needed a break. Is that so hard to understand?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You are not a monster. Not even a little. What I see is someone who has been carrying an enormous load for a very long time — and still showing up. That takes real strength.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I don't know. Last week was just — it was bad. My daughter, she's twelve, she found out about the DUI and she wouldn't talk to me. Three days. Wouldn't even look at me at dinner.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those three days of silence from her... what was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. Honestly, that was harder than anything the court did. She's old enough to understand, you know? And she just looked — disgusted. And I kept thinking, like... what am I doing? Is this really what I want her to see from me?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Her silence landed in a way the court order just couldn't reach.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Way harder. I mean... I keep telling myself I have it under control. But after that I just — I don't know. I'm not sure I believe that anymore. Like maybe I've been saying that to myself for a while and it's just... not true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture the kind of mom you want her to remember — what does she look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who... held it together. Someone she can be proud of. Not someone she has to be embarrassed by, or worried about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I try to bring together what I've been hearing today? You came in not wanting to be here — and that makes complete sense given everything. You've been doing it all on your own for years, and the wine was how you got through the nights. And then this week, your daughter's silence cracked something open. The part of you that wants to be the mom she's proud of — that part is speaking pretty loudly right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's it. I don't want to lose them. That's the one thing I can't — that's just not an option for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That love for them — that's something real to build from. So I'm just wondering, with everything you've shared today... is there one small thing, just one, that feels even a little bit possible to try this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not keeping wine in the house. Like if it's not just sitting there I can't automatically reach for it. I don't know if that'll fix anything but... I want to try something. I actually do.
